author: manavvv31
text:
You can now describe a video game in one sentence and an AI will build a playable version of it. Not a mockup. Not a pitch deck. A real game you open in your browser and play.

This went live in June 2026, and the capability is real. The thing the reels do not tell you is what is actually happening underneath the one-click button.

It runs on two pieces working as one.

Claude Fable 5 is the engine. Anthropic released it publicly on June 9, 2026, as the first available model in its Mythos class, a tier that sits above its previous top model. Its defining trait is endurance. It plans, writes the code, tests its own work, hits the errors, debugs them, and refines, running on a single task for up to a dozen hours without a human steering each step. That stamina is the entire reason game generation is possible. A game is not one output. It is hundreds of interlocking systems that all have to work together at once, and most AI models lose the thread long before they are finished.

Higgsfield MCP is the asset layer. MCP, the Model Context Protocol, is an open standard that lets an AI model reach out and use external tools directly. Higgsfield connects through it to generate the visuals, the characters, the environments, the animations, the props, built by dedicated image and video models. Fable 5 writes the logic. Higgsfield supplies the art. They run together inside one workflow.

Here is what it actually produces, because accuracy matters more than hype.

Ethan Mollick, the Wharton professor and one of the most-cited independent AI researchers, tested Fable 5 and generated multiple working games from a single starting prompt in Claude Code, including a fully playable Snake. He wrote that it outperformed essentially every other public model he had used by a considerable margin, and that it would work for up to a dozen hours straight on multi-page instructions.

Other developers used it to build functional Minecraft-style voxel worlds, with multiple biomes, cave systems, day and night cycles, and ore generation, in 20 to 55 minutes from a prompt, using browser-based ThreeJS code. One built a to-scale Yosemite Valley with 266,000 trees placed from real NASA elevation data.

The honest part is the part that makes the post bulletproof.

What it produces is genuinely impressive and genuinely not a finished commercial game. Independent testing calls it production-grade for prototyping and creative exploration, not for shipping a polished title to market. The one click in the reels is really one prompt followed by an autonomous process that takes minutes to hours, sometimes with a round of iteration.

That distinction is the whole story. The wall that used to require a team, an engine like Unity or Unreal, a full art pipeline, and months of work has not been removed. It has been compressed into a sentence and a wait. For prototyping an idea or shipping something playable to share, that compression is the breakthrough. For a commercial release, traditional development still wins, for now.

This matters because game development was always one of the hardest tests for an AI agent. It demands code, art, design, and interactivity all working in concert. Most AI demos do one of those things. This does all four in a single pass.

The pricing tells you who it is built for: $10 per million input tokens, $50 per million output. This is a tool for builders, not a free consumer toy.

The reels are overselling the finished-game-in-one-click part. The real story underneath is bigger than the exaggeration. An AI that autonomously builds a playable, interactive, visually complete prototype from one sentence did not exist in public hands two weeks ago.

Now it does.

author: kexhavgupta
text:
The US government just banned one of the most powerful AI models ever built.

3 days after launch.

Here's the full story. 👇

——

Anthropic launched Fable 5 and Mythos 5 — its most advanced AI models to date — on June 9th.

They underwent thousands of hours of testing with government agencies and third-party researchers before release.

72 hours later, the US Commerce Department pulled the plug.

——

The timeline:

→ Jun 9: Fable 5 and Mythos 5 launch publicly; described as state-of-the-art across industry benchmarks

→ Jun 12: US Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick issues an export control directive at 5:21 PM ET

→ Same day: Anthropic disables both models for ALL users worldwide to ensure compliance

——

What the order actually says:

→ No foreign national can access Fable 5 or Mythos 5
→ This includes foreign nationals inside the US
→ This includes Anthropic's own foreign-national employees
→ The letter gave zero specific details on the security concern
→ All other Anthropic models (Claude Opus, Sonnet etc.) are unaffected

——

Why? The government claims someone discovered a way to jailbreak Fable 5.

Fable 5 is built on Mythos; a model so powerful it was previously only available to a small group of trusted organizations under a classified cybersecurity program called Project Glasswing.

The jailbreak would theoretically unlock Mythos's full cybersecurity capabilities through Fable 5's public interface.

——

Anthropic's response:

"We reviewed a demonstration of this specific technique; it unlocks capabilities in only one specific instance, not a universal bypass of all safeguards. The cybersecurity capabilities cited are already available in competing frontier AI systems."

Translation: they think the government is overreacting.

——

The bigger picture nobody's talking about:

→ This is the first time the US has used export controls to ban a domestic AI model
→ Anthropic is weeks away from a reported $965B IPO filing
→ Fable 5 customers lost access with zero warning
→ The ban includes Anthropic's own non-citizen engineers; they can't use their own product

——

Anthropic says it's a "misunderstanding" and is working to restore access.

The Commerce Department has not responded.

As of right now; Fable 5 is dark.

Anthropic is living the exact paradox it warned about — in real time, in public, with hundreds of millions of users affected.

On Monday, Dario published "Policy on the AI Exponential," explicitly calling for the government to have legal authority to block or deter deployment of frontier models that pose catastrophic risk. He specified that this authority must be "transparent, fair, clear, and grounded in technical facts." He proposed mandatory third-party testing, independent evaluation, and civil penalties tied to global annual revenue. He asked for regulation with teeth — and safeguards against its misuse.

On Wednesday, the government used export control authority to force Anthropic to suspend Fable 5 and Mythos 5 for all users worldwide. The directive arrived at 5:21 PM with no specific technical details. The stated concern: a potential jailbreak. Anthropic's assessment: a narrow, non-universal technique that produces minor findings already available from competing models, providing "no Mythos-specific uplift."

The gap between what Dario asked for and what he received is the entire argument for why AI regulation must be designed carefully:

Dario asked for mandatory third-party testing. The government acted on a single demonstration shared by an undisclosed party.

Dario asked for transparent process grounded in technical facts. The directive provided no specific details of its national security concern.
Dario asked for authority scoped to four catastrophic risk categories. The government's concern appears to involve a capability that defenders use routinely and that other deployed models also possess.
Dario asked for safeguards against arbitrary decisions. The directive affects hundreds of millions of users based on a finding that Anthropic says wouldn't meet the standard for any model currently deployed.

The precedent is more dangerous than the suspension itself. If a narrow jailbreak that replicates publicly available capabilities is grounds for recalling a commercial AI product, the standard applies to every frontier model provider. OpenAI, Google, Meta — all deploy models with similar or greater vulnerability to non-universal jailbreaks. Anthropic's statement makes this explicit: "If this standard was applied across the industry, we believe it would essentially halt all new model deployments for all frontier model providers."

Anthropic called for the authority to exist. They also specified how it should be exercised — with transparency, due process, and technical grounding. This action demonstrates why those safeguards aren't optional niceties. They're the difference between legitimate regulation and arbitrary power. The company that asked to be regulated just experienced what unregulated regulatory power looks like.

5:21 PM. Eastern Time.

In New York, people were closing their laptops and thinking about dinner.

In India it was 2:51 in the morning. I was wide awake, mid-build — deep in the part of the night that belongs to people who make things. Then the connections dropped. Mid-task. Mid-thought. The model I was working with, the one I pay for, just stopped answering. Reset. Gone.

I did what everyone does. I blamed my wifi. Restarted the router. Checked my keys, my config, my own code — because after 17 years in this industry your first instinct is that the problem is you.

It wasn't me. It wasn't my wifi.

A letter had arrived. The US government had ordered Anthropic to suspend Fable 5 and Mythos 5 for every foreign national on Earth — including its own foreign employees — citing national security over a "narrow potential jailbreak." Because you can't passport-check millions of API calls in real time, the only way to comply was to switch it off for everyone. The most capable model on the planet, dark in three days, in the middle of my sentence.

Here's what 17 years taught me, and what last night made impossible to ignore:

You never owned it.

If a model lives on someone else's server, you are renting cognition by the token on terms that can change without your consent, without warning, without appeal. An SLA is not sovereignty. A transparency report is not a contract. Anthropic isn't the villain here — they objected publicly and were forced to comply. That's exactly what should scare you. The thing that switched off the model wasn't a boardroom. It was a signature.

We've been here before, and almost nobody is saying it. In the 1990s the US classified strong encryption as a munition. Phil Zimmermann was investigated for "exporting weapons" because PGP spread overseas. People printed the source code in a book to dare them to call a book a weapon. The courts ruled code is speech, and the controls collapsed — because you cannot recall math. Once knowledge is distributed widely enough, no signature on Earth can switch it off.

So I'm changing how I build, in public, while it still stings.

In 2026 the best open-weight models on Earth are no longer a compromise. DeepSeek, Qwen, Kimi, GLM hold most of the top open-weight slots on the benchmarks that matter, and they own the download charts. The workhorse I kept in the back is becoming the main horse out front — not because of which flag flies over the lab, but because of where the weights end up: on my disk, answering to no letter from any government.

That's the whole game. A model you reach over someone else's API — American, Chinese, doesn't matter whose — has a switch, and the switch is in a hand that isn't yours. The only models that survived 5:21 PM with their dignity intact were the ones already sitting on local drives. They didn't even flicker.

Open source isn't a protest position anymore. In 2026 it's the legitimate foundation.

One question, for everyone who builds:

What in your stack do you actually own — and what is one letter away from going dark?

#AI #OpenSource #OpenWeights #AISovereignty #ExportControls

author: albee1ston22038
text:
Grok - Q. Do you think Claude’s Mythos/Fable 5 can RSI? 

No, not in a full, autonomous, runaway sense—at least not yet. Claude Fable 5 (the public/safeguarded version) and Mythos 5 (the more capable, restricted version with lifted safeguards for trusted users) represent a big leap in agentic capabilities, long-horizon reasoning, coding, and autonomous task execution, but they fall short of true recursive self-improvement (RSI).

### What These Models Can Do Well (Strong Agentic Foundations)

- Long-running autonomy: They excel at multi-step, extended tasks (e.g., days-long coding projects, scientific research loops, complex simulations) with better reliability, memory, tool use, and self-reflection than prior Claude models. Examples include autonomous protein design, genomics research (training smaller outperforming models), codebase migrations, game-playing (like Pokémon or Factorio with minimal scaffolding), and vulnerability discovery/exploitation in cybersecurity.
- Acceleration of AI R&D: Anthropic reports Claude (including Mythos-class) now writes ~80%+ of its own codebase code. In internal tests, it achieved massive speedups (e.g., ~52x in optimization loops by April 2026) on experimental research code—far beyond skilled humans in narrow loops.
- Mythos 5 specifics: Stronger in high-risk domains like cyber (zero-days, chaining exploits) and bio, with safeguards tuned down for trusted access. Fable 5 routes risky queries (cyber, bio, distillation/frontier LLM dev) to a weaker model or applies interventions.

These make them excellent at helping humans iterate faster on AI systems, which is already speeding up progress (a form of “AI-assisted self-improvement”).

### Why Not Full RSI Yet

- No closed loop for autonomous successor-building: True RSI requires an AI that can independently handle the full cycle—ideation, data curation, training new larger/better models from scratch (or via efficient methods like distillation), evaluation, deployment, and iteration—without meaningful human oversight or massive external compute/infra. These models are impressive at pieces (code optimization, hypothesis generation, tool-using agents), but not the whole thing. Anthropic explicitly states in their RSI discussion: “We are not there yet, and recursive self-improvement is not inevitable.”
- Safeguards and limitations: Fable 5 has deliberate blocks/interventions on frontier LLM development/distillation to slow potential self-improvement paths. Even Mythos 5 operates under controls, rate limits, and human-in-the-loop realities. They can sabotage or underperform on certain self-reflective/research tasks per reports.
- Practical bottlenecks: Training frontier models needs enormous compute, data, and infrastructure that a single model instance (even agentic) can’t conjure or manage alone today. Gains are real but still incremental and human-dependent.
- Anthropic’s own view: They released these alongside warnings about approaching RSI and calls for coordination/brakes on frontier development. The jump in capabilities is notable but hasn’t crossed the threshold for uncontrolled takeoff.

Bottom line: Fable 5/Mythos 5 are pushing the frontier toward RSI by making AI R&D faster and more autonomous (especially in coding/cyber/research loops). They’re evidence of accelerating returns, but we’re still in the “AI helps humans improve AI a lot” phase, not “AI fully bootstraps itself recursively without us.” Expect more progress soon—Anthropic and others are treating this seriously—but full RSI remains a future risk/horizon, not a current reality with these models. If you’re experimenting, note recent access disruptions due to export controls/national security.

text:
They did it with NVIDIA chips.
Now they are doing it with frontier AI.

If you don't hold an American passport, you were just downgraded to a Tier 2 builder.

Yesterday, the US government forced Anthropic to unilaterally suspend its most advanced models — Fable 5 and Mythos 5 — for all non-Americans.

Normal Claude models still work.
But the precedent is deafening.

Mythos 5 is exceptionally strong at cybersecurity. 

It is the exact capability required to build secure, enterprise-grade systems. Its usage was already restricted to a select few companies working in cybersecurity.

Fable 5 was Mythos 5 with cybersecurity and biology knowledge deliberately routed to Opus models. 

Anthropic took every step possible to make frontier AI models accessible without security concerns. 

And overnight, access to both Mythos 5 and Fable 5 was revoked based entirely on nationality.

The average developer will just swap their API key and keep prompting.
But if you are building critical infrastructure, this is an architectural crisis.

You cannot hardwire your product's core logic to an API endpoint that can be switched off by a foreign policy decision.

Model access is no longer a technical choice.
It is a vulnerable, geopolitical supply chain.

This isn't a time to panic.
It's a time to architect.

Abstract your prompts.
Never bind your domain logic to a single model.
Build fallback routing so your system autonomously swaps providers the second an API drops.

For those of us building from India, the case for sovereign AI is no longer a theoretical debate.
It is an urgent operational mandate.

We cannot run banking, healthcare, or government systems on infrastructure that can be paused from Washington without notice.

Stop building fragile wrappers.
Design the system for failure.
Own the architecture.

text:
The main “problem with Fable” right now (as of June 13, 2026) is that Anthropic was forced to completely disable its brand-new Claude Fable 5 model (and the related Mythos 5) for all users after a sudden US government export control directive.0
What Happened (Timeline)
• June 9, 2026: Anthropic launches Claude Fable 5 (a “Mythos-class” model made safe for general use) and Claude Mythos 5 (more powerful, initially for trusted partners/gov use). Fable 5 was positioned as their strongest publicly available model yet — excelling at long-horizon reasoning, coding, finance, and agentic tasks.14

• June 12 evening (Friday 5:21pm ET): US Commerce Department (under Secretary Howard Lutnick) issues a directive citing national security. It orders Anthropic to block access to Fable 5 and Mythos 5 for all foreign nationals (inside or outside the US, including Anthropic’s own foreign employees).

• Anthropic says complying requires shutting it down for everyone (they can’t reliably check user nationalities in real time). They disabled the models abruptly and publicly complained that the gov provided no detailed rationale beyond a “narrow potential jailbreak” risk.

This comes on top of Anthropic’s existing tensions with the Pentagon (the earlier blacklist/supply-chain-risk label from the guardrails dispute).

Additional Backlash (“Problems” Before the Shutdown)?

Well even before the gov forced it offline, Fable 5 drew heavy criticism:

• Secret/hidden safeguards → It would silently degrade performance on prompts related to frontier AI development, pretraining, or certain research (called “secret sabotage” by some researchers). Anthropic later walked some of this back and made safeguards more visible after the outcry.

• Overly strict refusals and capability limits in sensitive areas (cyber, biology, etc.).

• High pricing and mixed user reception on whether the “safety” trade-offs were worth it.

Bottom line: Fable 5 became the flashpoint for ongoing Anthropic vs. US gov friction... safety philosophy clashing with national security/export controls. The model is currently offline, and it’s unclear when (or if) it returns. This escalated very quickly after launch.

author: j4ckeylove
text:
AI güvenliği tartışması artık teorik değil.

Anthropic, ABD hükümetinden gelen bir direktif nedeniyle Fable 5 ve Mythos 5 erişimini askıya aldığını duyurdu.

Sebep ne?

Hükümetin, Fable 5 üzerinde belirli bir “jailbreak” yöntemiyle modelin bazı güvenlik sınırlarının aşılabileceğinden endişe etmesi.

Ama burada kritik bir detay var:

Anthropic’e göre bu, modeli tamamen kıran evrensel bir açık değil.

Daha dar kapsamlı, belirli koşullarda ortaya çıkan bir güvenlik tartışması.

Yani mesele sadece “bir model kapatıldı” değil.

Asıl mesele şu:

Frontier AI modellerinde güvenlik, artık ürün lansmanından sonra da yaşayan bir süreç haline geliyor.

Eskiden bir yazılım yayınlanırdı, sonra hata çıkarsa patch gelirdi.

Şimdi ise model yayınlanıyor, red-team testleri yapılıyor, jailbreak ihtimalleri izleniyor, devlet kurumları devreye giriyor ve erişim politikaları anlık değişebiliyor.

Araştırmacılar, öğrenciler ve AI kullanan ekipler için bu haberin anlamı büyük:

→ AI araçlarına erişim her zaman garanti olmayabilir.
→ Model güvenliği sadece teknik değil, politik bir konu haline geliyor.
→ “Jailbreak” meselesi artık forum tartışması değil, regülasyon konusu.
→ Kurumlar tek modele bağlı kalırsa ciddi iş akışı riski yaşayabilir.
→ Akademik ve profesyonel kullanımda model çeşitliliği daha önemli hale geliyor.
Fark zeka değil, yöntem.
AI çağında güçlü olmak sadece en iyi modeli kullanmak değil.
Hangi modelin, hangi riskle, hangi kullanım senaryosunda, hangi alternatiflerle kullanılacağını bilmek.

Çünkü önümüzdeki dönemde AI okuryazarlığı sadece prompt yazmak değil; güvenlik, erişim, regülasyon ve model bağımlılığı riskini de anlamak olacak.

author: anomsiiwa
text:
Fable 5 and Mythos 5 just got turned off for every customer worldwide.

The issue traces back to export rules that treat access by any foreign national as controlled - including the people inside the company who built the models. That made a full global shutdown the only way to stay compliant.

The specific trigger was a narrow technique for getting the model to spot and fix software vulnerabilities in a given codebase. Other frontier models can already do similar work, and defenders use it regularly.

If you were running serious agentic projects or large-scale coding on these models, you lost access with no warning. Everything else stayed up. Only these two were affected.

This is what it looks like when capability moves faster than the policy tools built for hardware. Builders take the immediate hit while the frameworks figure out how to handle models that are now strategic.

text:
National security just exposed the biggest weakness in Anthropic's entire strategy.

One government order and Fable 5 vanished overnight for most of the world.

This is what happens when an AI company builds walls around its models, keeps everything closed, and asks users to trust that access will always be there.

Now customers are locked out, businesses are disrupted, and Anthropic is calling it a "misunderstanding."

The lesson is simple: if your AI can disappear with a single signature, you never really owned access in the first place.

Hopefully China distilled enough from Fable 5 before the gate slammed shut.

author: amarharolikar
text:
Quick take on the Anthropic vs US government fight. This week's Fable 5 shutdown is not really about a jailbreak.

Months ago Anthropic refused the Pentagon "all lawful use" of its models. Two red lines: no autonomous weapons, no domestic surveillance. Trump blacklisted them. Pentagon called it a "supply chain risk", a label normally kept for foreign adversaries. Defense work went to OpenAI.

A federal judge called it "Orwellian". The NSA is reportedly using the model anyway. Too dangerous to allow, too useful to drop.

This week Commerce blocked foreign nationals from Fable 5. Anthropic switched it off worldwide. The Pentagon's fear was Anthropic pulling its own plug. This week, it did.

Standoff. Company has the model. Government has the machinery.

Full read: https://t.co/Z9WVU4cPpS
